daily_reality.summary: Orthotists design and fit orthopedic braces/splints; prosthetists design and fit artificial limbs. Work split between clinical patient care (assessment, fitting, follow-up) and lab fabrication (casting, molding, assembly). ~10,100 practitioners nationwide.
typical_tasks: Evaluate patients and take measurements/impressions for device fitting
Design orthoses (braces) or prostheses (artificial limbs) based on physician prescriptions
Fabricate devices using thermoplastics, carbon fiber, acrylic, epoxy resins
Cast plaster molds or capture digital scans of affected limbs
Fit and adjust devices on patients — check alignment, comfort, function
Train patients in device use, care, and maintenance
Collaborate with physicians, physical therapists, and rehabilitation team
Use CAD/CAM software for digital design and modification
Document patient assessments and treatment progress in EMR

deadlines.device_delivery: Typically 2-6 weeks from initial assessment to delivery

daily_reality.seasonality: Relatively steady year-round. Some seasonal patterns: increased orthotics needs for sports injuries in spring/fall, prosthetics demand consistent. Medicare/insurance renewal cycles can affect Q4-Q1 ordering.

regulatory.summary: Requires master's degree from CAAHEP-accredited program plus 12-18 month NCOPE-accredited residency. National certification through ABC or BOC. ~20 states require state licensure. ISPO international accreditation recognizes US pathway as meeting highest standards.

key_laws.name: American Board for Certification (ABC)
key_laws.description: Primary certifying body — offers CO (Certified Orthotist), CP (Certified Prosthetist), CPO (dual) credentials

key_laws.name: NCOPE (National Commission on Orthotic and Prosthetic Education)
key_laws.description: Accredits residency programs; CAAHEP accredits academic programs

key_laws.name: State Licensure Laws
key_laws.description: ~20 states require state licensure; others rely on national certification

requirements: Bachelor's degree with prerequisites (biology, chemistry, physics, anatomy)
Master's degree from CAAHEP-accredited O&P program (includes 500+ clinical hours)
12-month NCOPE-accredited residency (per discipline) or 18 months for dual CPO
Pass ABC or BOC certification examinations

regulatory.continuing_education: Required for certification renewal; ABC requires CE credits every 5-year cycle; attendance at AAOP/AOPA meetings common

tools.summary: Transitioning from traditional plaster casting and hand fabrication to digital CAD/CAM workflows. 30% of prostheses now incorporate CAD/CAM (up from 23% in 2015). 3D printing emerging but not yet mainstream for definitive devices.

primary_tools.name: CAD/CAM Systems (Qwadra, formerly Rodin4D/Vorum)
primary_tools.description: Leading digital design and manufacturing platform for O&P — 97% of practitioners report positive patient care impact

primary_tools.name: 3D Scanners
primary_tools.description: Handheld and stationary scanners for digital limb impressions — replacing plaster casting. Some work with iPhone/iPad.

primary_tools.name: Traditional Fabrication Tools
primary_tools.description: Drills, sanders, grinders, vacuum forming equipment, ovens — still essential for many devices

primary_tools.name: CNC Carvers
primary_tools.description: Computer-controlled carving machines for producing positive models from digital designs

secondary_tools: 3D printers (emerging — Fused Deposition Modeling, SLS for socket production)
Alignment tools and gait analysis systems
Materials: carbon fiber, polypropylene, silicone, titanium components
pain_points: CAD/CAM adoption slower for orthotics than prosthetics
Software user-friendliness not optimized for direct device construction
High cost of digital scanning and CNC equipment
Insurance reimbursement doesn't always cover digital workflow costs
Learning curve for transitioning from manual to digital fabrication

terminology.summary: Rich specialized vocabulary covering anatomical levels of amputation, device types, biomechanical concepts, and fitting terminology. Heavy abbreviation use in clinical notes and insurance coding.

terms.AFO: Ankle-Foot Orthosis — brace for lower leg and foot
terms.KAFO: Knee-Ankle-Foot Orthosis — brace for entire leg
terms.SMO: Supramalleolar Orthosis — ankle/foot device below malleoli
terms.socket: The part of prosthesis that fits over the residual limb
terms.pylon: Structural component connecting socket to foot/knee unit
terms.check socket: Transparent test socket for initial fitting assessment
terms.L-codes: HCPCS Level II codes for O&P billing (L0000-L9999)
terms.donning/doffing: Putting on / taking off a prosthesis or orthosis
terms.alignment: Angular relationship of prosthetic components for optimal gait
terms.suspension: How prosthesis stays attached to residual limb
terms.myoelectric: Prosthetic hand/arm controlled by muscle electrical signals

career_psychology.summary: Meaningful career restoring mobility and independence. Master's degree now required (raised from bachelor's). 12% projected job growth (faster than average). Moderate salary with strong purpose-driven satisfaction. Workforce shortage creates job security.
career_path: Bachelor's degree with science prerequisites (4 years)
Master's degree in O&P from CAAHEP-accredited program (2-3 years)
Staff orthotist or prosthetist in clinical setting
fears: Insurance reimbursement cuts (L-code denials, prior auth hassles)
Liability for device failure or patient injury
Keeping up with rapidly changing technology (CAD/CAM, 3D printing)
Physical demands of lab work (standing, lifting, repetitive motions)
motivation: Life-changing impact — restoring mobility and independence
Combination of clinical care and hands-on craftsmanship
Strong interpersonal relationships with patients over long treatment
Growing field with strong job security
burnout_factors: High patient loads due to workforce shortage (60% demand vs supply gap by 2025)
Physical demands of fabrication and fitting
Emotional weight of working with amputees and trauma patients
Balancing clinical care with business management

community.summary: Two main organizations: AAOP (for individual practitioners, research) and AOPA (for businesses, 2,000+ facilities). Major conferences in February/March (AAOP) and September (AOPA National Assembly). Growing community with strong professional identity.

associations.name: American Academy of Orthotists and Prosthetists (AAOP)
associations.type: Professional association for individual O&P practitioners

associations.name: American Orthotic & Prosthetic Association (AOPA)
associations.type: Trade association for O&P businesses (2,000+ facilities)

events: AAOP Annual Meeting & Scientific Symposium (Feb/Mar — 190+ sessions)
AOPA National Assembly (September — largest O&P trade show, 100,000 sq ft exhibit)
ABC Exam Preparation Seminars (held at AAOP meetings)
online_communities: O&P Edge (oandp.com) — industry news and community
O&P professional groups on LinkedIn and Facebook
Amputee Coalition — patient advocacy with professional overlap

market.summary: Strong growth outlook: 13% projected job growth 2024-2034 (much faster than average). Significant workforce shortage — 60% demand-supply gap projected. Aging population driving demand. ~10,100 jobs with ~900 new openings annually.

job_outlook.workforce_gap: 60% higher demand than supply projected by 2025

demand_drivers: Aging baby boomer population (diabetes, cardiovascular disease = limb loss)
Increasing diabetes prevalence (leading cause of amputation)
Active lifestyle expectations driving orthotic demand
Advancing technology making devices more functional
market_trends: CAD/CAM adoption accelerating (30% prostheses, growing for orthotics)
Consolidation of O&P practices into larger groups
Medicare reimbursement policies under constant scrutiny
